subject: biology
prompt: The wheel shows the four **life processes**. Which of them removes harmful waste products from the body?

image.alt: Four life processes around a wheel: nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion

options.text: Nutrition
Respiration
Transportation
Excretion

hint: Think of what happens to the by-products that cells cannot use.
explanation: When cells use food and oxygen to release energy they create by-products that are useless or even harmful. Removing these wastes from the body is **excretion**. **Nutrition** brings in food, **respiration** uses oxygen to break food down for energy, and **transportation** moves food, oxygen and wastes between parts of the body. All four are maintenance processes that go on even when we are asleep.

subject: biology
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A virus particle that is inert outside a cell and becomes active once inside a living cell

assertion: There is a debate about whether viruses are truly alive.
reason: Viruses show no molecular movement until they infect a cell.
hint: Biologists say invisible molecular movement is needed for life.
explanation: Both statements are true and R explains A. Living things must keep repairing their ordered structures, so molecules must keep moving inside them. A virus shows **no molecular movement** until it enters a host cell, which is partly why people argue about whether it is truly alive.

subject: biology
prompt: A human is a large multi-cellular organism. Why is simple **diffusion** not enough to meet its oxygen needs?

image.alt: A single cell beside a block of many cells

options.text: Oxygen is not soluble in body fluids at all
Many cells are not in direct contact with the surroundings, so oxygen would reach them far too slowly
Diffusion works only for carbon dioxide, not for oxygen
Cells in multi-cellular organisms do not need oxygen

hint: Compare a single cell with the cell in the middle of a big block of cells.
explanation: In a single-celled organism the whole surface touches the environment, so diffusion is enough. In a large body most cells are **far from the surface**, so simple diffusion cannot supply them. That creates the need for specialised organs and a **transport system**. Oxygen does dissolve and diffuse, and cells certainly need it, so the other options are false.

subject: biology
prompt: Select **all** the things that are needed for photosynthesis.

image.alt: A green plant in sunlight taking in carbon dioxide and water and releasing oxygen while making glucose

options.text: Carbon dioxide
Water
Chlorophyll
Sunlight
Oxygen
Starch

hint: Raw materials, the light source and the green pigment are needed. Starch and oxygen are not raw materials here.
explanation: Autotrophs take in **carbon dioxide and water** and, in the presence of **sunlight and chlorophyll**, convert them into carbohydrates. **Oxygen** is released as a by-product, and **starch** is the stored form of the carbohydrate not used at once, so neither is an input.

subject: biology
prompt: Arrange the events of photosynthesis in the order in which they occur.

image.alt: A green plant in sunlight taking in carbon dioxide and water and releasing oxygen while making glucose

items.text: Light energy is converted to chemical energy and water molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen
Carbohydrate not used at once is stored as starch
Chlorophyll absorbs light energy
Carbon dioxide is reduced to carbohydrates

hint: Energy is captured first, then used to split water, and only then is CO2 reduced.
explanation: The chapter lists (i) absorption of light energy by chlorophyll, (ii) conversion to chemical energy and **splitting of water** into hydrogen and oxygen, and (iii) **reduction of carbon dioxide** to carbohydrates. The carbohydrates not used immediately are stored as **starch**. These steps need not follow each other instantly: desert plants take in CO2 at night and make an intermediate that is acted on by energy absorbed during the day.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the **stoma**. It is the tiny pore through which gases move in and out of a leaf.

image.alt: Cross-section of a leaf showing layers, a vein and a stoma with CO2 entering and O2 leaving

hint: Look for the small gap between two bean-shaped cells in the lower surface.
explanation: A **stoma** is a tiny pore on the leaf surface, flanked by two **guard cells**. Carbon dioxide enters and oxygen leaves through it. The layers above are epidermis and mesophyll cells, which have no such gap.

subject: biology
prompt: A **variegated leaf** (green in the middle, white at the edge) is kept in sunlight. Then it is decolourised (its colour is removed) in alcohol. Finally, it is dipped in dilute iodine. Which picture shows the expected result?

options.text: Whole leaf blue-black

image.alt: A leaf after the iodine test

options.text: Only the green part blue-black

image.alt: A leaf after the iodine test

options.text: Only the white edge blue-black

image.alt: A leaf after the iodine test

options.text: No colour change anywhere

image.alt: A leaf after the iodine test

hint: Starch turns blue-black with iodine, and only chlorophyll-containing cells photosynthesise.
explanation: Only the part that **had chlorophyll** made starch in sunlight, so only the formerly green region turns **blue-black** with iodine. The white edge has no chlorophyll, so no photosynthesis and no starch. This shows that **chlorophyll is essential** for photosynthesis.

subject: biology
prompt: Put the steps of the starch-test activity in the correct order.

image.alt: A leaf in a test tube of alcohol standing in a beaker of hot water over a flame so the green colour is removed

items.text: Dip the leaf in boiling water
Keep the plant in a dark room for three days
Heat the leaf in alcohol in a water bath to remove chlorophyll
Keep it in sunlight for about six hours and pluck a leaf
Dip the leaf in dilute iodine and observe the colour

hint: The plant must first use up its old starch.
explanation: Three days in the dark use up the starch already present. Sunlight lets photosynthesis make fresh starch. **Boiling water** softens the leaf, then **hot alcohol (in a water bath)** removes chlorophyll so the colour change is visible. Alcohol is never heated directly because it is flammable. Finally **iodine** shows where starch is present.

subject: biology
prompt: Two plants were kept in the dark. Then they were placed under bell-jars in sunlight. Jar (a) had a watch-glass of **potassium hydroxide (KOH)**. Jar (b) had no KOH. Which leaf shows **more starch**, and why?

image.alt: Two bell jars over potted plants: one with a dish of potassium hydroxide inside, one without

options.text: Leaf (b), because KOH in jar (a) absorbs carbon dioxide so less photosynthesis happens there
Leaf (a), because KOH adds nutrients
Both the same, because starch forms in the dark
Leaf (a), because KOH absorbs oxygen

hint: What does KOH remove from the air in the jar?
explanation: **KOH absorbs carbon dioxide**. The plant in jar (a) has no CO2, so it cannot photosynthesise and makes little or no starch. The plant in jar (b) has CO2 and makes starch. This shows that **carbon dioxide is essential** for photosynthesis.

subject: biology
prompt: What makes a **stomatal pore open**?

image.alt: A stomatal pore shown open between two guard cells and closed between two guard cells

options.text: Water flows out of the guard cells and they shrink
The guard cells photosynthesise and divide
Carbon dioxide pushes the guard cells apart
Water flows into the guard cells and they swell

hint: Think about a balloon filling with water.
explanation: The opening and closing of the pore is a function of the **guard cells**. When water flows **into** them they **swell** and the pore opens. When they lose water and shrink, the pore closes. The plant closes the pores when it does not need CO2 because large amounts of water can also be lost through them.

subject: biology
prompt: In this **Amoeba**, tap the **food vacuole**. This is where complex food is broken down into simpler substances.

image.alt: An amoeba with pseudopodia, a nucleus, a food vacuole holding a food particle and a contractile vacuole

hint: It is the round bubble that holds a green food particle.
explanation: Amoeba takes in food with finger-like **pseudopodia** that fuse over the food particle to form a **food vacuole**. Inside it, complex substances are broken down into simpler ones that **diffuse into the cytoplasm**. The nucleus controls the cell but does not hold food.

subject: biology
prompt: Arrange the stages of **nutrition in Amoeba**.

image.alt: An amoeba with pseudopodia, a nucleus, a food vacuole holding a food particle and a contractile vacuole

items.text: Complex substances are broken down inside the vacuole
Finger-like extensions of the cell surface surround the food particle
Simpler substances diffuse into the cytoplasm
A food vacuole forms around the food
Undigested material is moved to the surface and thrown out

hint: Food must be captured before it can be digested, and waste leaves last.
explanation: The extensions (**pseudopodia**) fuse over the food to form a **food vacuole**. Complex substances are digested into simpler ones, which **diffuse into the cytoplasm**. Whatever remains undigested is moved to the surface of the cell and expelled.

subject: biology
prompt: Match each organism with how it gets its food.

image.alt: Four heterotrophs: an amoeba engulfing food, a paramoecium with cilia, a bread mould on bread, and a cuscuta climbing a plant

right.text: Finger-like extensions fuse over food to form a food vacuole
Cilia sweep food to one particular spot on the cell
Breaks down food outside its body, then absorbs it
Draws nutrition from a living plant without killing it

hint: Parasites live on a host; fungi digest outside the body.
explanation: **Amoeba** engulfs food with pseudopodia. **Paramoecium** has a definite shape and takes in food at a specific spot, to which **cilia** move it. **Bread mould** (a fungus) breaks food down outside the body and absorbs it. **Cuscuta** is a **parasite**: it takes nutrition from a plant without killing it, as ticks, lice and leeches do from animals.

subject: biology
prompt: In Activity 5.3, iodine is added to both tubes. Tube **A** (starch + saliva) stays brownish. Tube **B** (starch only) turns blue-black. What does this show?

image.alt: Two test tubes: starch with saliva stays brown after iodine; starch without saliva turns blue-black

options.text: Starch dissolves in water, so tube A had none left
Iodine detects sugar, not starch
Salivary amylase in the saliva broke the starch down into simple sugar
Saliva contains no enzyme, so the starch in tube A was unchanged

hint: Blue-black with iodine means starch is still present.
explanation: Iodine turns **blue-black** with starch. Tube B (no saliva) still has starch, so it turns blue-black. Tube A does not, so its starch is gone: saliva contains the enzyme **salivary amylase**, which breaks starch, a complex molecule, into simple sugar. Starch does not simply dissolve away, and iodine tests for starch, not sugar.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the **stomach**. Here, gastric glands release hydrochloric acid, pepsin and mucus.

image.alt: Human digestive system with a food ball travelling from mouth to anus

hint: It is the large, expanding bag just below the food-pipe.
explanation: The **stomach** is a large muscular organ that expands as food enters. Its **gastric glands** release hydrochloric acid, the protein-digesting enzyme **pepsin**, and mucus. The liver makes bile, and digestion is completed in the small intestine.

subject: biology
prompt: What is the role of **hydrochloric acid** in the stomach?

image.alt: Gastric glands in the stomach wall releasing hydrochloric acid and pepsin, with a protective mucus layer

options.text: It creates an acidic medium that helps the enzyme pepsin to act
It digests fats into fatty acids
It makes the food alkaline
It protects the stomach lining from digestion

hint: The acid helps an enzyme. Which one?
explanation: Hydrochloric acid creates the **acidic medium** in which **pepsin**, the protein-digesting enzyme, works best. **Mucus**, not the acid, protects the stomach lining. Fats are digested later in the small intestine, where the food is made **alkaline** (by bile), not in the stomach.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the **pancreas**. It secretes (releases) pancreatic juice, which contains **trypsin** and **lipase**.

image.alt: Human digestive system with a food ball travelling from mouth to anus

hint: It lies just below the stomach and sends its juice to the small intestine.
explanation: The **pancreas** secretes pancreatic juice with **trypsin** (digests proteins) and **lipase** (breaks down emulsified fats). The liver, which makes bile, is the large dark organ beside the stomach.

subject: biology
prompt: Which statement correctly describes what **bile juice** from the liver does?

image.alt: A large fat globule, and many small globules after bile salts act on it

options.text: It digests proteins into amino acids
It converts starch into glucose
It makes the food more acidic so that pancreatic enzymes can act
It makes the acidic food from the stomach alkaline and breaks fat globules into smaller ones

hint: Think of how soap breaks up grease.
explanation: The food from the stomach is acidic, but pancreatic enzymes need an **alkaline** medium, so **bile makes it alkaline**. Bile salts also **emulsify** large fat globules into small ones, giving enzymes more surface to act on, just like soap on dirt. Bile contains no digestive enzyme, so it does not digest proteins or starch.

subject: biology
prompt: Match each enzyme with its job.

image.alt: Human digestive system with a food ball travelling from mouth to anus

right.text: Breaks starch into simple sugar in the mouth
Digests proteins in the acidic stomach
Pancreatic enzyme that digests proteins
Breaks down emulsified fats

hint: Match by where each enzyme is made: salivary glands, stomach, pancreas.
explanation: **Salivary amylase** (saliva) acts on starch. **Pepsin** (gastric glands) digests proteins in the acid of the stomach. **Trypsin** (pancreatic juice) also digests proteins, while **lipase** breaks down fats that bile has emulsified. The intestinal juice finally converts proteins to amino acids, carbohydrates to glucose, and fats to fatty acids and glycerol.

subject: biology
prompt: A cow has a much **longer small intestine** than a tiger. What is the best reason for this?

image.alt: A long coiled small intestine of a grass-eater beside a short small intestine of a meat-eater

options.text: Tigers do not digest food in the small intestine
Grass contains cellulose, which takes longer to digest, while meat is easier to digest
Cows eat less food than tigers
Cows swallow whole prey that must be broken down slowly

hint: Compare how hard grass and meat are to digest.
explanation: Herbivores eating grass need a **longer small intestine** to allow the **cellulose** to be digested. **Meat is easier to digest**, so carnivores like tigers have a shorter one. Both animals digest in the small intestine, so the idea that tigers do not is wrong, and prey swallowing is not how a cow feeds.

subject: biology
prompt: Which features help the **small intestine absorb** digested food? Select all that apply.

image.alt: A single villus of the small intestine with a capillary network and a lymph vessel in its centre

options.text: Very long and extensively coiled to fit in a compact space
Numerous finger-like villi that increase the surface area
Villi richly supplied with blood vessels
Gastric glands that release hydrochloric acid
Bile made inside its wall

hint: Think about surface area and carrying the food away.
explanation: The small intestine is the **longest part** of the canal, fitted into a small space by **coiling**. Its inner lining has **villi** that increase the surface area, and the villi are **richly supplied with blood vessels** that carry the absorbed food to every cell. Hydrochloric acid is made in the stomach and bile in the liver.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the **blood capillaries** in the villus. They carry absorbed food to the cells of the body.

image.alt: A single villus of the small intestine with a capillary network and a lymph vessel in its centre

hint: Look for the red loop running up and over the tip of the villus.
explanation: Villi are richly supplied with **blood capillaries** (red) which take the absorbed food to every cell, where it is used for energy, building new tissue and repair. The yellow central tube is a **lymph vessel**, which carries absorbed fat.

subject: biology
prompt: Food passes through these parts. Arrange them in order, from where food enters to where it leaves.

image.alt: Human digestive system with a food ball travelling from mouth to anus

items.text: Stomach
Mouth
Small intestine
Oesophagus (food-pipe)
Large intestine
Anus

hint: The alimentary canal is one long tube from the mouth to the anus.
explanation: Food is chewed and mixed with saliva in the **mouth**, passes down the **oesophagus**, is churned in the **stomach**, digested and absorbed in the **small intestine**, loses water in the **large intestine** and leaves through the **anus**, controlled by the anal sphincter.

subject: biology
prompt: Why does brushing the teeth **after eating** help to prevent tooth decay?

image.alt: A tooth covered with plaque where bacteria make acid that softens the enamel

options.text: It makes the saliva more acidic
It kills all bacteria in the mouth permanently
It hardens the pulp of the tooth
It removes plaque before bacteria can make acid that demineralises the enamel

hint: Plaque is a sticky film of bacteria and food particles.
explanation: Bacteria acting on sugars produce **acid** that softens the enamel. Masses of bacteria and food form **plaque**, which stops saliva from reaching the tooth to neutralise the acid. Brushing removes the plaque before the acid is made. If decay is untreated, microorganisms may reach the pulp and cause infection.

subject: biology
prompt: Exhaled air (air we breathe out) turns lime water **milky faster** than air pushed through with a pichkari. What does this show?

image.alt: Lime water turning milky when exhaled air is blown through it, compared with air pushed through with a pichkari

options.text: Exhaled air contains more oxygen
Lime water reacts only with moisture
Exhaled air contains more carbon dioxide than ordinary air
Ordinary air contains no gases

hint: Lime water turns milky with carbon dioxide.
explanation: Lime water turns **milky with carbon dioxide**. Breath makes it milky much faster, so exhaled air has a **higher CO2 content**: the CO2 comes from respiration in our cells. Ordinary air has only a little carbon dioxide, so it takes longer.

subject: biology
prompt: In Activity 5.5, yeast is put in sugar solution. A delivery tube from this set-up dips into lime water. What does the lime water show about **fermentation**?

image.alt: Yeast and sugar solution in a flask with a bent tube leading the gas produced into lime water that turns milky

options.text: Fermentation produces carbon dioxide, along with ethanol
Fermentation uses up carbon dioxide
Fermentation needs oxygen
Fermentation gives lactic acid and oxygen

hint: What turns lime water milky?
explanation: The lime water turns milky, showing that **carbon dioxide** is released. In yeast, glucose first breaks into **pyruvate**, which is converted into **ethanol and carbon dioxide** in the absence of oxygen. This is **anaerobic respiration**. Lactic acid forms in our muscles, not in yeast, and no oxygen is needed.

subject: biology
prompt: Match each step in the breakdown of glucose with where or when it happens.

image.alt: Flow chart: glucose to pyruvate, then three possible products: ethanol and carbon dioxide, lactic acid, or carbon dioxide and water

left.text: Pyruvate converted into ethanol and CO2
Pyruvate broken into CO2 and water

right.text: In the cytoplasm
In yeast, in the absence of air
In muscle cells that lack oxygen
In the mitochondria, in the presence of oxygen

hint: Only one step needs oxygen, and it happens in the mitochondria.
explanation: The first step, glucose to **pyruvate**, always occurs in the **cytoplasm**. Pyruvate becomes **ethanol and CO2** in yeast during fermentation (no air), or **lactic acid** in our muscles when oxygen is short. With oxygen, pyruvate is completely broken down in the **mitochondria** to carbon dioxide and water. Lactic acid is also a three-carbon molecule.

subject: biology
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A tall bar for the energy released in aerobic respiration and a short bar for anaerobic respiration

assertion: Aerobic respiration releases much more energy than anaerobic respiration.
reason: In aerobic respiration, pyruvate is broken down completely into carbon dioxide and water. This happens in the mitochondria.
hint: Complete breakdown extracts more energy from the same glucose.
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. In the aerobic pathway **pyruvate is fully broken down using oxygen**, so a lot more energy is released than in anaerobic pathways, where pyruvate is only partly converted (to ethanol or lactic acid). The energy is used to make **ATP**, the energy currency of the cell.

subject: biology
prompt: After sudden, very hard exercise, your muscles cramp (become tight and painful). Which substance builds up in the muscle cells and causes this?

image.alt: A working muscle that gets little oxygen, in which a substance made from pyruvate builds up

options.text: Ethanol
Carbon dioxide
Lactic acid
ATP

hint: Think of what pyruvate becomes when oxygen is short.
explanation: When muscle cells lack oxygen, pyruvate is converted into **lactic acid**, a three-carbon molecule. Its build-up in the muscles during sudden activity causes **cramps**. Ethanol is made by yeast, CO2 is a product of aerobic breakdown, and ATP is the energy currency, not a cause of cramps.

subject: biology
prompt: Which statement about **gas exchange in a plant** is correct?

image.alt: A leaf in sunlight by day and the same leaf at night

options.text: By day, O2 is the only gas exchanged and CO2 is never released
At night, plants release oxygen as the major event
Gases enter plants only through the roots
At night, CO2 release is the major exchange, since there is no photosynthesis

hint: Photosynthesis happens only in light, but respiration goes on all the time.
explanation: At night there is no photosynthesis, so **CO2 elimination** (from respiration) is the major exchange. By day, the CO2 produced in respiration is **used up** in photosynthesis, so there is no net release; instead **oxygen release** becomes the major event. Gases are exchanged across stems, roots and leaves, mainly via stomata.

subject: biology
prompt: **Aquatic animals** (animals that live in water) such as fish breathe much faster than land animals. Why?

image.alt: A fish taking in water through its mouth and passing it over the gills under the gill cover

options.text: The amount of oxygen dissolved in water is fairly low compared with that in air
Water is much thicker than air
Fish have no lungs, so they need more oxygen
Fishes' gills do not touch the water

hint: Compare how much oxygen is in air and in water.
explanation: The amount of **dissolved oxygen** in water is fairly low compared with the amount in air, so aquatic organisms have to take in more water, and breathe **faster**. Fishes take water in through the mouth and force it past the **gills**, where the dissolved oxygen is taken up by blood.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the **alveoli**. These are balloon-like structures where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged.

image.alt: Human respiratory system: nostrils, windpipe, bronchi, lungs with alveoli and the diaphragm

hint: Look for the tiny grape-like sacs at the ends of the smallest tubes.
explanation: Within the lungs the air passage divides into smaller and smaller tubes that end in balloon-like **alveoli**. Their walls have an extensive network of **blood vessels**, so this is where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it. Together they give a huge surface, about 80 m2 if spread out.

subject: biology
prompt: When we **breathe in**, which of these happen? Select all that apply.

image.alt: The ribs, lungs and diaphragm of the chest while breathing in, with air entering

options.text: The ribs are lifted
The diaphragm flattens
The chest cavity becomes smaller
Air is pushed out of the lungs
Air is sucked in and fills the expanded alveoli

hint: Breathing in makes more room inside the chest.
explanation: On breathing in we **lift our ribs and flatten the diaphragm**, so the chest cavity becomes **larger**. This sucks air into the lungs, which fills the expanded alveoli. A smaller cavity and air being pushed out belong to breathing out.

subject: biology
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A red blood cell picking up oxygen in the lungs and releasing it in the tissues

assertion: Large animals such as humans need a respiratory pigment such as haemoglobin.
reason: Diffusion alone would be far too slow to carry oxygen to all parts of a large body.
hint: Haemoglobin in the red blood cells has a very high affinity for oxygen.
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. In big bodies diffusion pressure alone cannot deliver oxygen; it would take years for oxygen to reach the toes. **Haemoglobin** in the **red blood corpuscles** takes up oxygen in the lungs and releases it in oxygen-poor tissues. Most carbon dioxide, being more soluble in water, travels dissolved in the blood.

subject: biology
prompt: Which of these does **plasma** carry in dissolved form? Select all that apply.

image.alt: A blood sample with straw-coloured plasma, red blood cells and platelets

options.text: Digested food
Carbon dioxide
Nitrogenous wastes
Oxygen
Platelets as dissolved molecules

hint: Oxygen travels in a different part of the blood.
explanation: **Plasma** is the fluid in which blood cells are suspended. It transports **food, carbon dioxide and nitrogenous wastes** in dissolved form (and salts). **Oxygen** is carried by the **red blood cells**, and platelets are cells, not dissolved substances.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the **left ventricle**. It is the thick-walled chamber that pumps oxygen-rich blood to the whole body.

image.alt: Sectional view of the human heart: four chambers, vena cava, pulmonary artery and aorta

hint: The ventricle on the same side as the aorta, with the thickest wall.
explanation: The **left ventricle** has the thickest muscular wall because it pumps oxygen-rich blood out to the body. The ventricles have thicker walls than the atria because they must pump blood into various organs. The right ventricle pumps blood only to the lungs.

subject: biology
prompt: Birds and mammals use a lot of energy to keep their body temperature steady. Which type of heart suits them?

options.text: Three chambers, with mixing of blood

image.alt: A three-chambered heart with one ventricle

options.text: Four chambers, fully separated right and left

image.alt: A four-chambered heart with a complete wall down the middle

options.text: Two chambers

image.alt: A two-chambered heart

options.text: A single tube

image.alt: A heart that is a single tube

hint: Think about why oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood should not mix.
explanation: Separating the right and left sides keeps **oxygenated and de-oxygenated blood from mixing**, allowing highly efficient oxygen supply. This suits **birds and mammals**, which constantly use energy to maintain body temperature. Amphibians and many reptiles have **three-chambered** hearts and tolerate some mixing, and fishes have only **two** chambers.

subject: biology
prompt: Start with blood coming back from the lungs. Arrange the path of blood through the heart.

image.alt: Blood pumped from the right side of the heart to the lungs and back to the left side, then from the left side to the body and back, so it passes through the heart twice

items.text: The left ventricle pumps the blood out to the body
The right ventricle pumps the blood to the lungs
Oxygen-rich blood from the lungs enters the left atrium
De-oxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium

hint: Atrium receives, ventricle pumps. Oxygen-rich blood is on the left.
explanation: Oxygen-rich blood reaches the **left atrium**, passes to the **left ventricle**, which pumps it to the body. De-oxygenated blood returns to the **right atrium**, passes to the **right ventricle**, and is pumped to the lungs. The blood goes through the heart **twice** in one cycle: this is **double circulation**.

subject: biology
prompt: A **vein** has thin walls and **valves**, so that blood flows only one way. Which picture shows a vein?

options.text: Tiny vessel, one cell thick

image.alt: A tiny vessel whose wall is one cell thick

options.text: Thick elastic wall, narrow channel

image.alt: A vessel with a thick, elastic wall and a narrow channel

options.text: Thin wall, wide channel, with valves

image.alt: A vessel with a thin wall, a wide channel and valves

options.text: Thick wall, wide channel, with valves

image.alt: A vessel with a thick wall, a wide channel and valves

hint: Veins carry blood that is no longer under high pressure.
explanation: **Veins** collect blood from organs and bring it back to the heart. The blood is no longer under high pressure, so they do not need thick walls, but they have **valves** to keep the blood flowing in one direction. **Arteries** (thick, elastic walls) carry blood away from the heart under pressure and **capillaries** (one-cell-thick walls) allow exchange with cells.

subject: biology
prompt: Match each part of the transport system with its function.

image.alt: A blood sample with straw-coloured plasma, red blood cells and platelets

right.text: Carries blood away from the heart under high pressure
Has valves so blood flows only towards the heart
One-cell-thick wall where materials are exchanged
Plug leaks by helping the blood to clot
Carries digested fat and drains excess fluid back to the blood

hint: Match structure to job: thick walls, valves, thin walls, clotting, tissue fluid.
explanation: **Arteries** have thick, elastic walls to take blood leaving the heart under high pressure. **Veins** have valves. **Capillaries** have walls one cell thick so materials can be exchanged with the cells. **Platelets** circulate and plug leaks by helping the blood clot. **Lymph** (tissue fluid) carries digested and absorbed fat from the intestine and drains excess fluid from the tissues back into the blood.

subject: biology
prompt: A healthy adult's blood pressure is about **120/80 mm Hg**. What does the **120** mean?

image.alt: A cuff on the arm connected to a pressure gauge whose needle swings up to the normal reading

options.text: The diastolic pressure in the veins
The pressure in the atria while they relax
The pressure in the capillaries during ventricular relaxation
The pressure of blood in the arteries during ventricular contraction (systolic pressure)

hint: Systole means contraction; diastole means relaxation.
explanation: The pressure in an artery during **ventricular systole** (contraction) is the **systolic pressure**, about 120 mm Hg. The pressure during ventricular **diastole** (relaxation) is the **diastolic pressure**, about 80 mm Hg. Blood pressure is measured with a **sphygmomanometer** and is much greater in arteries than in veins.

subject: biology
prompt: During the **day**, the stomata are open. At this time, what is the main force that moves water up the xylem?

image.alt: A tree with water moving up the xylem from the roots and water vapour leaving the leaves

options.text: Root pressure
Translocation through phloem
Transpiration pull, the suction created by evaporation from leaves
Active uptake by guard cells

hint: Water evaporating from the leaf pulls the water column behind it.
explanation: **Evaporation of water** from leaf cells creates a **suction (transpiration pull)** that draws water up the xylem. During the day it is the major force, whereas **root pressure** matters more at night. Transpiration also helps absorb water and minerals and regulates temperature.

subject: biology
prompt: Two pots are covered with plastic sheets and kept in sunlight. One pot has a **plant**. The other has a **stick**. Droplets form only in the pot with the plant. What does this show?

image.alt: Two pots under plastic sheets in sunlight; water droplets collect only inside the sheet over the pot with a plant

options.text: Plants lose water vapour through their leaves (transpiration)
The soil gives out more water under a plant
The stick absorbs the water
Plastic sheets produce water

hint: The soil was covered in both pots, so evaporation from it was blocked.
explanation: The soil is covered in both pots, so evaporation from the soil is stopped. Water vapour lost through the stomata of the **plant** condenses on the plastic as droplets. The stick does not lose water, so its pot stays dry. This is **transpiration**, the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts.

subject: biology
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Sugar made in a leaf loaded into the phloem using energy and carried to a growing bud or root

assertion: Transport in phloem needs energy. But transport in xylem can be explained mostly by simple physical forces.
reason: Sucrose is moved into the phloem using energy from ATP. This raises the osmotic pressure and draws water in.
hint: Think of how the phloem moves material according to the plant's needs.
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. In **translocation**, materials like sucrose are moved into the phloem using **ATP**. This raises the osmotic pressure, so water flows in, and the pressure pushes the material to tissues with lower pressure, such as buds in spring. Xylem transport depends mainly on transpiration pull and root pressure.

subject: biology
prompt: Which statements about **xylem and phloem** are correct? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Two tubes in a stem: xylem fed from the roots and phloem fed from the leaves

options.text: Xylem carries water and minerals taken from the soil
Phloem carries the soluble products of photosynthesis (translocation)
Transport in phloem occurs only upwards
Translocation takes place in sieve tubes with the help of companion cells
Xylem carries food in both directions

hint: One tissue moves water up; the other moves food up and down.
explanation: **Xylem** conducts water and minerals from the roots. **Phloem** carries the products of photosynthesis, amino acids and other substances in **both upward and downward** directions through sieve tubes with companion cells. So it is not only upward, and xylem does not carry food.

subject: biology
prompt: In a nephron, blood is filtered in a **cluster of thin-walled blood capillaries**. Tap this cluster.

image.alt: A nephron: Bowman's capsule round a capillary cluster, a long tube with a capillary network and a collecting duct

hint: It is the red knot sitting inside the cup-shaped capsule.
explanation: In the kidney the basic filtration unit is a **cluster of very thin-walled blood capillaries** (the glomerulus) enclosed by the cup-shaped end of a coiled tube, the **Bowman's capsule**, which collects the filtrate. Along the tube, glucose, amino acids, salts and much water are selectively **reabsorbed**.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the **ureter**. It is the tube that carries urine from the kidney to the urinary bladder.

image.alt: Human excretory system: two kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder and urethra

hint: There is one for each kidney, running down to the bladder.
explanation: Urine made in the **kidneys** passes through the **ureters** into the **urinary bladder**, where it is stored until released through the **urethra**. The bladder is muscular and under nervous control, so we can usually control the urge to urinate.

subject: biology
prompt: A healthy adult's kidneys filter about **180 L** of fluid a day. But they pass out only **1.5 L** of urine. How much of the filtrate is **reabsorbed** (taken back)?

image.alt: A tall bar for 180 litres of filtrate made daily and a tiny bar for the one or two litres of urine passed

hint: Reabsorbed = filtered minus excreted.
explanation: $$180\ \text{L} - 1.5\ \text{L} = 178.5\ \text{L}$$ is reabsorbed in the tubules. Traps: 181.5 L comes from **adding** instead of subtracting, 120 L from **dividing** $180 \div 1.5$, and 1.5 L is just the urine volume. The amount of water reabsorbed depends on how much excess water there is in the body and how much dissolved waste has to be excreted.

subject: biology
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: An artificial kidney: blood flows through tubes bathed in dialysing fluid and wastes diffuse out

assertion: In an artificial kidney (haemodialysis), wastes pass from the patient's blood into the dialysing fluid.
reason: The dialysing fluid has the same osmotic pressure as blood. But it has no nitrogenous wastes. So wastes move out of the blood by diffusion.
hint: Diffusion moves substances from where there is more to where there is less.
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. The blood flows through tubes with a **semi-permeable lining** inside the dialysing fluid, and nitrogenous wastes **diffuse** out because the fluid has none. Unlike a real kidney there is **no reabsorption** in this process.

subject: biology
prompt: Plants use different methods to get rid of waste. Match each method with its description.

image.alt: A plant that stores wastes in vacuoles and gums, drops old leaves and releases some wastes into the soil

right.text: Wastes are stored inside the cells
Wastes stored in old parts are shed
Stored especially in old xylem
Some wastes are excreted into the surroundings
Excess water is lost as vapour

hint: Plants can shed parts, store wastes and release them.
explanation: Plants use **different strategies** from animals. Many wastes are stored in **cell vacuoles**, and waste can be stored in **leaves that fall off**. Others are stored as **resins and gums**, especially in old xylem, and some are excreted into the **soil**. Excess water is lost by **transpiration**, and oxygen itself can be thought of as a waste product of photosynthesis.
